title: Dorando: Won and Lost in the Marathon
subtitle: In 1908 a small Italian runner entered the Olympic stadium in first place. He did not finish the way he started — and the world has never forgotten it.
intention: you'll follow a true race story and tell stories of your own with confident narrative tenses, so you can describe any event — a race, a match, a hard day — clearly and with feeling.
warmup: Have you ever carried on with something long and difficult when part of you wanted to stop? What kept you going?
Why do people choose to do things that are hard on purpose — races, climbs, long challenges? What do they get from it?
Think of a sporting moment you remember vividly. Where were you, and what happened?

vocab.heading: A · What do they mean here? Work it out from the context
vocab.intro: Read the sentence, work out the word in bold, then reveal. Say your guess out loud first.

items.sent: A beginner who starts too fast usually can't keep the same pace for the whole race.
items.meaning: pace (noun) — the speed at which you run or move, often measured in minutes per kilometre: a steady pace.

items.sent: Marathon runners need great stamina: the ability to keep going for hours without becoming exhausted.
items.meaning: stamina (noun) — physical or mental energy that lets you continue an effort for a long time.

items.sent: Many runners say they hit the wall at around thirty kilometres: suddenly their legs feel empty and every step is a struggle.
items.meaning: hit the wall (idiom) — to reach the point in a long effort where your energy runs out and you can hardly continue.

items.sent: She finished in 1 hour 52 minutes, a new personal best, six minutes faster than her previous race.
items.meaning: personal best (noun) — your own fastest or highest result so far, often shortened to PB.

vocab.heading: B · More from the race
vocab.intro: Same method: guess from the sentence, then reveal.

items.sent: On the final bend he overtook two runners and moved into third place.
items.meaning: overtake (verb) — to pass someone who is moving in the same direction: overtook, overtaken.

items.sent: After thirty kilometres she took the lead and nobody could catch her.
items.meaning: take the lead (phrase) — to move into first place; to be in front.

items.sent: Exhausted, he staggered across the finishing area, barely able to keep his balance.
items.meaning: stagger (verb) — to walk or move unsteadily, as if about to fall, because you are very tired, ill or hurt.

vocab.heading: C · After the race
vocab.intro: These three words are the heart of the story. Guess, then reveal.

items.sent: Halfway up the hill the runner collapsed and lay on the road until the medical team reached him.
items.meaning: collapse (verb) — to fall down suddenly because you are very weak, tired or ill.

items.sent: The team was disqualified because one of its members had broken the rules, so its result was removed.
items.meaning: disqualify (verb) — to officially remove someone from a competition for breaking the rules.

items.sent: The coach lodged a protest with the judges, arguing that the result should be changed.
items.meaning: protest (noun) — here, a formal complaint made to the officials of a competition.

vocab_use: Describe a time you went at the wrong pace — too fast or too slow — in a race, a project or a journey.
Which job or hobby needs the most stamina? Explain why.
Have you ever felt a sporting result was unfair and wanted to protest? What happened?
story_heading: Dorando Pietri and the 1908 Olympic Marathon

story.heading: Part 1 — A very hot afternoon
paras: On 24 July 1908, the Olympic Games were being held in London, and the marathon was about to start. The route began at Windsor Castle and finished inside the new stadium at White City, so that the royal family could watch the beginning and the crowd could watch the end. The distance was about 26 miles and 385 yards — roughly 42 kilometres. The usual explanation is that this odd measurement came from the exact length of that route, and it was later adopted as the standard marathon distance.

More than fifty runners set off in heat that was severe for the time. Many of them started too quickly. As the afternoon went on, they began to fall away, one after another, and ambulances collected the ones who had stopped at the side of the road.

Among the runners was Dorando Pietri, a twenty-two-year-old from the small Italian town of Carpi, who worked in a sweet shop. He was short and light, and few people had heard of him. Instead of racing at the front, he had run at a careful pace for most of the way. While the leaders were fading, he was quietly moving up through the field.
checks: Where did the race start and where did it finish, and why was that route chosen?
What happened to many of the runners as the afternoon went on?
How did Dorando run for most of the race, and what was he doing while the leaders faded?
answers: It started at Windsor Castle and finished in the stadium at White City, so that the royal family could see the start and the crowd the finish.
They had started too fast in the heat, so they slowed down, fell away and some had to be taken off the road by ambulance.
He ran at a careful, steady pace and was moving up through the field while the leaders were getting weaker.
story.discuss: Which is the better plan for a long race — a fast start or a careful pace? What do you do in other situations, like exams or long projects?

story.heading: Part 2 — The stadium
paras: By the time the leaders were approaching the stadium, Dorando had overtaken most of them and had taken the lead. He entered the arena at White City in first place, to the cheers of about 75,000 people. But he looked terrible. He had been running for nearly three hours, and he had clearly hit the wall.

Then he turned the wrong way. Officials ran to him and pointed him in the right direction. A few steps later his legs gave way and he collapsed on the track. He got up, staggered forward, and fell again. Most accounts say he fell five times in the last few hundred metres.

Doctors and officials crowded round him. The spectators were shouting. And at some point, while Dorando was lying on the track, someone took his arm and lifted him to his feet. Supported on both sides, he staggered towards the line. He crossed it in 2 hours 54 minutes and 46 seconds, with the stadium roaring.
checks: What was the situation when Dorando entered the stadium?
What mistake did he make, and how did the officials respond?
How did he get across the finishing line?
answers: He was in first place and 75,000 people were cheering, but he was completely exhausted — he had hit the wall.
He turned the wrong way; officials ran to him and turned him round to face the right direction.
Officials and doctors helped him up and supported him on both sides, so he staggered across the line with their help.
story.discuss: You are one of the officials standing next to him. Do you help him? What would you do in that moment, and why?

story.heading: Part 3 — The decision
paras: The crowd had been watching a man win the Olympic marathon. But almost at once, the American team lodged a protest. Their runner, Johnny Hayes, had come in about half a minute later, and they argued that Dorando had been helped to the finish. The rules said that he should have run the race without assistance.
The judges agreed. Dorando was disqualified, and the gold medal went to Hayes. Dorando was taken to the medical room.

That might have been the end of the story. Instead, the public had already decided who the real hero was. The newspapers wrote about him for days — the writer Arthur Conan Doyle, the creator of Sherlock Holmes, reported on the race and described the final lap in detail. The next day Queen Alexandra presented Dorando with a special gilded silver cup. A song, “Dorando”, was written about him. Later he made a living by running exhibition races in several countries.
Hayes kept his gold medal, and few people argue that the decision was legally wrong. And yet more than a century later, it is Dorando's name that most people remember.
checks: Why did the American team protest?
What was the judges' decision, and who received the gold medal?
What happened to Dorando afterwards, even though he had been disqualified?
answers: They argued that Dorando had been helped over the finishing line, which the rules did not allow.
The judges upheld the protest: Dorando was disqualified and the gold medal went to Johnny Hayes.
He became famous: newspapers praised him, the Queen gave him a silver cup, a song was written about him, and he ran exhibition races for money.
story.discuss: The judges applied the rules correctly, yet most people remember Dorando, not Hayes. Why? What does that say about what we admire?

grammar.name: Narrative Tenses
grammar.lead: A good story keeps different times in order — what was happening in the background, what happened next, and what had already happened. Four tenses do that job. Look at how the story above used them.
notes: 1 · Past simple — the main events, in order. “Dorando entered the stadium. He turned the wrong way. Officials pointed him in the right direction.” Each verb moves the story forward.

2 · Past continuous — the background, or an action in progress. “The spectators were shouting while the doctors were helping him.” Use it for the scene, or for a longer action that something else interrupts: “While he was lying on the track, someone lifted him up.”
3 · Past perfect — what had already happened before the main events. “He had started carefully, so he still had some energy.” “The leaders had run too fast.” It takes us one step back in time.

4 · Past perfect continuous — the long action leading up to a moment. “He had been running for nearly three hours when he entered the stadium.” It stresses how long something went on, and often its effect.

5 · Choosing between them. Ask: Is this a step forward in the story (past simple)? Is it the scene or an action in progress (past continuous)? Did it happen before the story's moment (past perfect)? Did it go on for a long time before it (past perfect continuous)?

6 · The traps. When he had entered the stadium, the crowd cheered — if the events happen one after the other, use past simple for both: “When he entered the stadium, the crowd cheered.”  He was falling five times → “He fell five times” (a completed series of events, not a scene in progress).

exercises.heading: Which tense? Put the verb in brackets into the correct form
exercises.intro: Read the whole sentence first. Decide: main event, background, earlier event, or long action before a moment.
items: 1. By the time the runner reached the stadium, the sun ___ (beat) down on the course for three hours.
2. The first runner ___ (arrive) while the band ___ (play).
3. He ___ (not eat) anything since breakfast, so he felt weak at the 30-kilometre mark.
4. While the officials ___ (argue), the second runner ___ (cross) the line.
5. When I ___ (finish) the race, my friends ___ (wait) for me with a bottle of water.
answers: 1. had been beating (a long action before the moment: “for three hours”)
2. arrived / was playing (main event, then the background scene)
3. had not eaten (earlier than the weak feeling at 30 km)
4. were arguing / crossed (background action, then a completed event)
5. finished / were waiting (main event, then the scene they were in)

exercises.heading: Fix the story
exercises.intro: Each sentence contains one tense mistake. Rewrite the whole sentence correctly.
items: 1. He fell five times before somebody has helped him.
2. The leaders were running too fast, so they were exhausted by the time they reached the hills.
3. When Dorando was entering the stadium, 75,000 people stood up and cheered. (The second event follows the first.)
4. The judges decided that he broke the rules.
5. He was running for nearly three hours when he entered the stadium.
answers: 1. He fell five times before somebody helped him.
2. The leaders had run too fast, so they were exhausted by the time they reached the hills. (They ran fast before they became exhausted.)
3. When Dorando entered the stadium, 75,000 people stood up and cheered.
4. The judges decided that he had broken the rules. (The rule-breaking came before the decision.)
5. He had been running for nearly three hours when he entered the stadium.

exercises.heading: Tell it in order
exercises.intro: Here are some notes. Write one sentence for each, using the tense the note suggests. Then say the whole story aloud.
items: 1. (earlier event) Dorando / train carefully / for months / before the Games → ___
2. (background) the stadium / be / full of noise / when he / arrive → ___
3. (main event) officials / lift / him / to his feet → ___
4. (earlier event) the American team / already / lodge / a protest / by the evening → ___
5. (long action) he / run / for almost three hours / when he / collapse → ___
answers: 1. Dorando had trained carefully for months before the Games. (or: had been training)
2. The stadium was full of noise when he arrived.
3. Officials lifted him to his feet.
4. By the evening, the American team had already lodged a protest.
5. He had been running for almost three hours when he collapsed.

grammar.closing: Now tell the whole Dorando story aloud in under a minute, with at least one example of each of the four tenses.

deeper.heading: Going deeper — the race, the rules and the numbers
deeper.lead: The story of Dorando is about more than one man's bad luck. It raises questions about fairness, effort and what we count as winning — and it also explains something about the distance runners train for today.

blocks.heading: Where do 42 km and 21 km come from?
paras: The marathon distance was not fixed until after 1908. After the London Games it was gradually standardised at 42.195 km — 26 miles 385 yards — which is the length of that Windsor-to-stadium route. A half marathon is simply half of it: 21.0975 km, or 13.1 miles.

Today a half marathon is one of the most popular distances in the world. It is long enough to demand real training, but short enough that many ordinary runners can complete it within a few months of preparation.

items.q: What is the exact length of a half marathon in kilometres?
Which event in the story is the usual explanation for the marathon's odd length?
items.a: The 1908 London Olympics: the route from Windsor Castle to the stadium.

items.q: Say the sentence in the past perfect: “They ran too fast, and then they became tired.”
items.a: They had run too fast before they became tired.

blocks.heading: Was it fair?
paras: People have argued about the 1908 decision for over a century. Both sides have a real case.

pairs.b: The rule was clear: no assistance. If officials are allowed to help the leader but not the others, the race is no longer equal. Johnny Hayes had run the whole distance on his own legs.

pairs.a: The case for keeping his victory
pairs.b: He was the first to arrive. The officials were trying to save him from harm, and he had not asked for help. Punishing him for being rescued seems harsh.

blocks.heading: Language for talking about a race
paras: These phrases work for any race — your own, or one you watched. Complete the sentences from memory, then reveal.

items.q: Which word completes the phrasal verb meaning “to start a race or journey”: “We set ___ at nine o'clock.”
“I was ___ for the last two kilometres.” (hang on — in the past continuous)
items.a: hanging on — meaning I was barely able to keep going.

items.q: “I ___ a personal best.” (made / set — which verb goes with the noun?)

discuss: Is finishing a race more important than winning it? Does it depend on the race?
Should rules be applied strictly even when the result seems unfair? Think of an example outside sport.
Why do crowds often cheer louder for the person who is struggling than for the winner?

speak.useful: “By the time I …, I had already …” · “While I was …, … happened” · “I had been … for … when …” · “The moment I will never forget is when …” · “Looking back, …”

paras: Describe a time you wanted to stop but kept going. What was happening, and what made you continue?

tasks.label: Task 2 — The event
paras: Tell the story of a race, match, trip or event you took part in: the build-up, the main moment and what happened afterwards.

tasks.label: Task 3 — The preparation
paras: Describe something you trained or prepared for over weeks or months. What did you do, and did it go as planned?

paras: Choose a side: was Dorando's disqualification fair? Argue your case in two minutes, then argue the other side.

final: Dorando is remembered more than the man who officially won. What makes someone memorable — results or the way they achieve them?
The Americans followed the rules and protested. Were they right to do so, even though the crowd loved Dorando?
Is it better to be a famous loser or an unknown winner? Does the answer change as you get older?
From memory: retell the Dorando story in five sentences, using past simple, past continuous, past perfect and past perfect continuous.
